title: Generous Dealing of Yahya bin Khalid

full_text:
Yahya bin Khalid, the patriarchal head of the illustrious Barmecide family, was celebrated throughout the Islamic world for his exquisite tact, boundless charity, and princely magnanimity.

One morning, an impoverished gentleman of noble lineage named Mansur entered Yahya’s reception hall. Mansur had inherited vast estates, but famine and crop failures had reduced him to absolute destitution; he was heavily indebted to creditors and had pawned his family’s ancestral silver to buy bread.

Too proud to beg publicly in the marketplace, Mansur stood quietly among the petitioners, his head bowed with sorrow.

Yahya bin Khalid noticed his downcast eyes and noble bearing. Instead of offering him a humiliating handout of copper before the crowd, Yahya summoned Mansur to his private library. He embraced him warmly, sat him upon his own divan, and asked: 'Brother, how may the house of Barmak serve a noble soul like you?'

Mansur wept and confessed: 'My lord, I owe twenty thousand dinars to demanding creditors, and my household faces starvation.'

Yahya took a reed pen and wrote three letters: the first to the governor of Egypt, requesting him to grant Mansur a fertile estate; the second to the chief merchant of Damascus, directing him to clear all Mansur's debts; and the third to the imperial treasurer of Baghdad, granting Mansur a monthly pension of three hundred dinars.

Before Mansur could speak, Yahya handed him a heavy purse of five thousand gold dinars for travel expenses, saying with deep humility: 'Take this modest gift, my brother, and forgive me that my assistance is so small. It is we who are indebted to you for granting us the honor of serving an honorable man.'

Mansur walked out into the sunshine with tears of gratitude, marveling at how true nobility bestows charity with such grace that it elevates the receiver rather than humbling him.
moral: Nobility uses its influence to restore the dignity of the fallen without making them feel humiliated.
